stances.claim: There are really no illegitimate children — only illegitimate fathers and mothers — because children bear no fault in their conception and birth; our law's labeling is a legal necessity, not a moral judgment on the children themselves.

stances.claim: Under the Revilla Law, express recognition through a signed birth certificate, notarized document, or written instrument — not mere implied acknowledgment — is required for an illegitimate child to use the father's surname and thereby access surname, support, and succession rights.
stances.rhetorical_move: legal-precision clarification: distinguishing express from implied recognition as the operative legal trigger

one_paragraph_summary: Using the Ramgen Bautista murder case -- allegedly masterminded by siblings RJ and Ramona, with money rifts over the ailing Sen. Revilla Sr.'s unequal allowance distribution as the theorized motive -- as his entry point, Panganiban surveys the legal rights of illegitimate children under Philippine law. He opens with his personal moral position: 'there are really no illegitimate children; there are only illegitimate fathers and mothers' who beget offspring outside valid marriage. Under the Civil Code and Family Code, illegitimate children use the mother's surname by default, but the 2004 Revilla Law (RA 9255 -- authored by the senator himself) allows use of the father's surname through express (not implied) recognition in a signed birth certificate, notarized document, or written instrument. Once expressly recognized, illegitimate children gain support rights (sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical care, education extending beyond majority, transportation -- proportional to the giver's means and the recipient's needs), and siblings of any filiation must support each other under the Family Code. On succession, recognized illegitimate children are compulsory heirs entitled to a legitime equivalent to one-half of what a legitimate child receives -- they cannot be disinherited from their legitime. Adopted and legitimated children (whose parents had no legal impediment to marry at the time of their conception) enjoy the same rights as legitimate children.
